sources.title: National Register of Historic Places listings in Miami
Wikipedia GeoSearch, 10 km around downtown Miami (25.7743, -80.1937)

stops.name: Freedom Tower
stops.description: Built in 1925 for the Miami News and later used to process Cubans fleeing the 1959 revolution, which is what made it a National Historic Landmark.

stops.name: Bayfront Park
stops.description: Thirty-two acres of public lawn on Biscayne Bay, open since March 1925, with Isamu Noguchi's Challenger Memorial standing at the southwest corner.

stops.name: Miami Circle at Brickell Point
stops.description: A 38-foot ring of postholes cut into the bedrock by the Tequesta as much as 2,700 years ago, reburied under limestone to protect it and marked at the mouth of the Miami River.

stops.name: Palm Cottage
stops.description: The last building in Miami with a direct tie to Henry Flagler, put up around 1897 for the men building his Royal Palm Hotel and moved to this park in 1980.

stops.name: Miami Tower
stops.description: Pei Cobb Freed stacked three glass tiers 625 feet up in 1987, and the LED system installed in 2012 repaints all three for the season or the holiday.

stops.name: Ingraham Building
stops.description: A 1927 office tower from the tail end of the land boom, listed on the National Register with the rest of the downtown core in 1989.

stops.name: Huntington Building
stops.description: Known for most of its life as the Consolidated Bank Building, a boom-era survivor a block off Flagler Street.

stops.name: Miami-Dade County Courthouse
stops.description: When this 28-story courthouse topped out in 1928 it was the tallest building in Florida and the tallest anywhere south of the Mason-Dixon line.

stops.name: Alfred I. DuPont Building
stops.description: Finished in 1939, the first skyscraper Miami raised after the bust of 1928, which makes it the city's monument to climbing back out.

stops.name: Olympia Theater
stops.description: John Eberson built this 1926 movie palace with a ceiling painted as an open night sky, one of only four atmospheric theaters left standing in Florida.

stops.name: Walgreen Drug Store
stops.description: A 1936 Streamline Moderne drugstore that has been a department store and, since 2023, a food hall named for Julia Tuttle and Henry Flagler.

stops.name: Shoreland Arcade
stops.description: Opened in 1925 at the peak of the land boom and later occupied by Dade Federal Savings, whose name it still answers to.

stops.name: Security Building
stops.description: Sixteen floors and 275 office suites raised in 1927 by the Dade County Security Company, which razed the hotel it already owned on this lot to make room.

stops.name: Old U.S. Post Office and Courthouse
stops.description: Miami's federal building of 1914, and the third floor is where the Weather Bureau sat when it put out the warnings for the Great Miami Hurricane of 1926.

stops.name: Gesu Church
stops.description: The oldest Catholic parish in Miami, holding services on this block since 1896, which is older than most of the streets around it.

note: Miami had never had a run. Fifteen stops, all verified against their own articles, all still standing and all visible from the street. The set is a tight downtown loop: Freedom Tower at the north end, Miami Circle at the river mouth in the south, the Flagler Street corridor in the middle, roughly 0.9 miles across at its longest and walkable end to end. Addresses come from the NRHP listing rows, not from coordinates. Every ZIP was looked up from the verified street address through the Census geocoder rather than derived from the city. One caveat on Bayfront Park: the park's own contact page gives 33132 while the City of Miami parks directory and the Census address file both give 33131, and I filed the 33131 that two of the three sources agree on. Dropped on distance rather than quality: the Lyric Theater at 819 NW 2nd Ave in Overtown, which is a strong Black-history stop but sits across I-95 and would stretch the loop past three miles, and Vizcaya, the Coconut Grove cluster and the Bacardi Complex, all several miles out. Also dropped a dozen near-identical 1920s office blocks on the same two streets, since a tour that names eight of them in a row stops being a tour.
